scope: Two new regular candidates and two proposed identities, ten exact image reviews. No runtime edits, publication or video mutation.

proposals.subject: Atlantic armored searobin
proposals.title: The third return
proposals.content: I thought he was stuck. Shook him off very carefully. He climbed back on. The third time I understood I was the place he was trying to get to.
proposals.review: NOAA explicitly reports the brittle star climbing onto the fish three times and the fish dislodging it. Careful intent and belated understanding are fictional. The exact frame shows the brittle star beside the long prongs; the documented sequence supplies the repeated contact. Do not claim the fish subsequently carried the star or that its behavior scientifically proves affection.

media.sourceTitle: The Armored Searobin and the Brittle Star
media.sourceCaption:
During the Océano Profundo 2015: Exploring Puerto Rico’s Seamounts, Trenches, and Troughs expedition, while exploring the top of a Late Oligocene to Pilocene platform carbonate sequence and traversed a relatively minor fault scarp. This fault is the easterly extension of an approximately 100-kilometer-long fault system that forms the northern wall of the rift between the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, when witnessed an unusual encounter.
Seeing two deep-sea animals interacting with each other is rare. What is particularly rare is when they behave the opposite of how we expect them to. As we approached this armored searobin, a brittle star climbed on top of it. We watched to see if the fish would try to eat the brittle star, but as it turns out, it just wanted to dislodge the extra baggage. The brittle star then proceeded to climb on top of the sea robin two more times…persistent little guy!
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Puerto Rico’s Seamounts, Trenches, and Troughs
media.visibleScene: Red armored searobin face at right with very long paired rostral prongs extending left beside a pink brittle star on tan sediment. Large dark eye, bony ridges and modified fin rays clear.

proposals.subject: Alaskan lithodid king crab
proposals.title: The next grip
proposals.content: Every time I loosened my claw, theirs moved with it. I thought we were about to let go. Then I felt the new grip. It took me several changes of position to stop treating each one as the end.
proposals.review: NOAA explicitly identifies mating. Overlapping limbs and claws are visible; the changing grips and emotional interpretation are fiction. No sex assignment, injury, fear diagnosis or physiological mating mechanism beyond source evidence. Nestor is the foreground left animal used for the avatar.

profiles.subject: Atlantic armored searobin
profiles.bio: An armored searobin. My visitors have their own ideas.

location.name: Deep seafloor near Mona Passage, northern Caribbean

profiles.body: Adult-sized red armored searobin with exceptionally long narrow paired rostral prongs, a large dark eye, bony head ridges and modified free fin rays. Species and reproductive sex unresolved. Do not substitute short-pronged Florida fish or Pacific Scalicus.
profiles.want: To help smaller neighbors while retaining a little room around himself.
profiles.fear: Mistaking a request for company for a creature in trouble.
profiles.flaw: Acts on an interpretation before waiting to see what the other animal does.
profiles.voice: Plain first-person Facebook accounts. Quick physical action followed by a belated correction; no species lectures.
profiles.history: First encounter is the repeatedly climbing brittle star. No youth, breeding, injury or death invented.

profiles.subject: Alaskan lithodid king crab
profiles.bio: A deep-sea king crab. Taking small changes personally.

location.name: Rocky deep slope in the Gulf of Alaska

profiles.body: Adult red spiny lithodid crab, compact oval speckled carapace, stout jointed spiny legs, small visible dark eyes and grasping claws. Source resolves Lithodidae only. Species and which photographed animal is male or female remain unresolved.
profiles.want: Close contact that survives an awkward adjustment.
profiles.fear: A loosening grip means the other animal is leaving.
profiles.flaw: Holds too firmly when uncertain, making the next movement harder for both.
profiles.voice: Short tactile admissions on Instagram; no armor/vulnerability stock joke or human anatomical substitution.
profiles.history: Mating encounter first. Nestor is the foreground left crab; partner is unnamed and ungendered. No eggs, parenthood or post-molt softness inferred.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: This lithodid crab was observed moving its body back and forth through the sediment, though the on-ship team was not sure exactly why it was doing so. Seen at a depth of 2,240 meters (7,349 feet) during the sixth dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: Pale orange lithodid face over sediment, very long slender claw tips and raised dark eyes. Source observed back-and-forth sediment movement; shape differs from the red compact mating pair.
sourceReview.dimensionsMeaning: Exact published image or video-poster asset dimensions measured from source bytes; no camera-original dimensions inferred.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: The king of Trinidad Slump? The focus of the fourth dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition was testing remotely operated vehicle systems by the Global Foundation for Ocean Exploration team. Part of the testing included flexing the zoom capabilities of vehicle cameras, giving us a close look at this king crab in the family Lithodidae at a depth of 2,413 meters (7,917 feet).
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: Sediment-coated dark red king crab with strong spikes and long antennae, California Trinidad Slump. Similar family does not prove same kind as the Alaskan mating pair; no distinct action in this portrait.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
A number of these unusual looking creatures were seen on the seafloor during Dive 09 of the 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration. These armored searobins (Triglidae) use modified fins to move across the seafloor and branched “whiskers” in front of their mouths to help them sense food. 
  Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: Pink armored searobin with short broad rostral projections, many long branched barbels and fins on sediment south of Florida Keys. Does not match Edgar narrow very long paired prongs.
sourceReview.dimensionsMeaning: Exact published image or video-poster asset dimensions measured from source bytes; no camera-original dimensions inferred.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
For today’s daily dose of deep-sea weird, meet the armored searobin! These unusual fish use modified fins to move across the seafloor and branched “whiskers” in front of their mouths to help them sense food. 
 This one was seen at 600 meters (1,970 feet) depth  during a dive  to explore an area south of the Florida Keys in the Straits of Florida.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: Another frontal view of the short-pronged Florida armored searobin on sediment. Same body incompatibility and no second event.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
During Dive 08 of the third Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition, a rarely observed aggregation of sea urchins ( Conolampas sigsbei ) was seen, much to the delight of scientists onboard and onshore. The urchins each appeared to have a cluster of debris on the apex of its body, leading scientists to liken them to “hats.” 
  Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
sourceReview.visibleScene: Small urchin aggregation behind a large Victorian Hat Party title overlay. Poster cannot be treated as an unmarked photograph.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Three individuals of a large group of sea urchins seen during Dive 08 of the third Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition. Note the debris “hats” directly on top of the body. Scientists commented that since each individual had debris in exactly this place, it was too consistent to be incidental.
Learn more

sourceReview.visibleScene: Three dome-shaped Conolampas urchins carry small debris piles at their apices on gray mud. Distinct anatomy, but a hats/costume joke would merely follow the source pun.
